headline: Firmus IPO failure is a pricing and execution verdict, not a verdict on AI demand; public investors will pay for capacity that is running and earning but discount capacity still to be financed, powered and built
reasoning: Noah Zuckerman argues the Firmus IPO failure reflects pricing and execution risk rather than weakening AI demand. The IPO price was nearly 3x the August ground price, which was simply too much for institutions. The binding constraint in the sector is power, not chips or financing, and converting a pipeline to gigawatt-scale coherent clusters involves significant uncertainty around grid equipment, permits and build risk. Institutions did not say no to the data centre build-out model, but said no to that price at that point in time.
quote: At Non-Public, our view really is the firm isn't a verdict on AI demand necessarily. It's a verdict on pricing and execution risk. So public investors will happily pay for capacity if it's running and earning, and they'll discount capacity that still has to be financed, powered and built. Ultimately, price here decides returns and nearly three X from two months ago in August on the ground price was just too much for investors to ask. Ultimately, the bottleneck in this industry is power, not chips in financing now, and delivery depends on grid equipment, cruise permits. There's a lot of uncertainty and execution risk to convert the pipeline, and investors are considering that heavily.
episode_title: Was the Firmus float flop a pricing problem?

headline: ASX structurally disadvantaged for large technology listings versus Nasdaq: smaller market, shallower capital, less specialist growth-investor base; local funds should not be expected to pay US-style multiples
reasoning: Zuckerman notes the ASX has genuine strengths but is a smaller market for large technology companies. The US offers deeper capital pools, more specialist investors and greater experience valuing growth companies. He does not expect ASX to close this gap quickly by asking local investors to pay US multiples, citing the Firmus episode as evidence that appetite for premium-priced growth is not there domestically. He references Hermes as another example of this dynamic.
quote: The SE has strengths, but it's a smaller market for large technology companies. And so the US just has deeper capital, specialist investors and more experienced in valuing growth. This is mitigated by adding depth of capital to ASX over time, which could contribute to more listings, but not by expecting local investors and funds to pay us multiples. Ultimately, as we saw with Hermes, and I think that we've seen that that appetite is not there with firms.
episode_title: Was the Firmus float flop a pricing problem?

headline: IPO pulled after institutions rejected the price; deploying 46MW is no small feat but building true gigawatt-scale coherent clusters is exponentially harder and unproven for this company
reasoning: Firmus attempted to list at nearly three times its August ground price, and institutional investors in the book-build rejected the valuation. While Firmus had deployed 46MW — a meaningful achievement — scaling to true gigawatt-level coherent clusters is exponentially more difficult. There is significant execution risk around grid, permits and financing. Zuckerman notes Firmus may now pursue a Nasdaq listing, which he sees as a rational response given deeper US capital markets for growth tech.
quote: deploying 46MW is no small feat, as firmus did, but building true gigawatt scale coherent clusters is exponentially harder and still to be determined if they could do that.
episode_title: Was the Firmus float flop a pricing problem?

headline: Highest-conviction 2027 themes follow the binding constraint: power and energy storage (photonics, optical interconnects, behind-the-meter on-site power) and orbital/space-based compute
reasoning: Zuckerman says the binding limit for AI scale-up in 2027 remains power, and that the key opportunities are in technologies that unlock more usable compute or deliver far more tokens per watt. His highest-conviction areas are photonics, optical interconnects, on-site behind-the-meter power and energy storage, as well as orbital and space-based compute. He frames these as following the constraint rather than chasing generic AI demand.
quote: So we're following the constraint in 2027. The binding limit right now is AI scale up. It's still power and technologies that unlock more usable lots or deliver far more tokens per what are the highest conviction areas were betting on. So that would be photonics, optical interconnects on site behind the meter, power and energy storage, as well as orbital and space based compute.
